about.scope: Barbican Estate numbered flat types, for tagging Frank Harris listings in flatview

how_numbering_works.summary: Each layout was given a number by the City Corporation when the estate was built. Agents use it as shorthand ("Type 20"). Codes follow rules (Barbican Living, interpretive, not an official City key).
rules: Number + single letter (1A, 2B, 8C, 4A): a tower flat in Cromwell, Lauderdale or Shakespeare Tower. Number = layout, letter A/B/C = which side of the triangular tower; A flats end in 1, B in 2, C in 3.
Letter-number-letter (F1A, F2C, P2A, M3B): North Barbican. F = studio/flat, P = penthouse, M = maisonette (letters not exclusive).
Number only (19, 20, 109): South Barbican terrace flat or mews house.
Number + H (35H): the "handed" mirror image of that type.
how_numbering_works.caveat: Rules come from the Barbican Living author (Rowallen Ltd), a resident site, not the City. Tower-type digit clusters (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) group variants such as water-tank floors (3A/3B/3C, 9A/9B/9C) and penthouses (4A/4B/4C).

barbican_living_original_estate.note: Counted from the type list on the page nav (1A ... P2B, incl. combined 63/64 and 67/68). Page text says "over a 100".

total_types.verdict: ~140 is real (City guidelines, Orazi book) but Barbican Living documents only 128 original types; the gap of ~12 is unexplained (possible variants/handed versions/one-offs). UNCERTAIN which is exact. Plus Frobisher Crescent (32 types, own x.y numbering) and Blake Tower (30, invented names) which are later conversions.

estate_totals.later_conversions: 69 flats in Frobisher Crescent, 74 in Blake Tower (ex-YMCA)
estate_totals.gap_note: Our per-type counts sum to 1,995 vs 2,014 official; 19 unaccounted (Postern "Maisonette" and "No. 3" rows lack type numbers, some blocks may have rows not captured). Treat counts as +/- small.

about.count_method: count = sum of the per-block "Total" column in Barbican Living block flat-types tables (url pattern https://www.barbicanliving.co.uk/blocks/<block>/flat-types/). Cross-checks: Type 20 = 54+59+36+48 = 197 and Type 21 = 54+48+36+48 = 186, matching Thomas Michael exactly; F1A 71, F2A 140, F2C 84, M2A 56, M2B 60, 26 = 42, 31 = 63 also match.

sizes.finding: No public source gives official floor area per type. Barbican Living deliberately gives no sizes for original types (plans are "illustrations and approximations only"). sqft fields are ranges from individual agent listings (n shown) and are INDICATIVE. Frobisher Crescent pages give per-type m2/sq ft; Blake Tower type names are the area in m2.
sizes.studio_dimensions: Barbican Living quotes City figures: all studio types share a 16'9" frontage; max depths F1A 10'6", F2A 19'3", F2B 19'6", F1D/F1E/P1D 18'0", 13 20'3" (https://www.barbicanliving.co.uk/studio-flats/).

(area in m2, invented by Barbican Living) collide with original types 48, 108 etc. Original type 108 = Willoughby penthouse; Blake 108 = 108 m2 two-bed. Tag by block first. Frobisher x.y types never collide. Agents also use the tower "4B/4C" for penthouse.

famous_or_sought_after.why: Most common (197); large L-shaped one-bed, sliding partition makes second sleeping area; described as "one of the most sought after one-bedroom lateral apartments" (agent).
Most common two-bed (186); similar size to Type 20.
Duplex penthouses with double-height living room, three bedrooms, roof terrace; 24 in total in Gilbert, Mountjoy, Seddon; "rarely available" (Frank Harris).
One-bed penthouse under barrel-vaulted roof; 64 in the four lakeside terraces.
Andrewes House lake-level garden flats: split-level living room, tall U-shaped lake window, some with private patios.
Brandon Mews houses: sub-podium, spiral stairs/split-level living; 26 houses. Lambert Jones Mews (Type 10, 8 houses) have double-height living rooms and garden access (Nicola Lee).
One each in Shakespeare, Cromwell and Lauderdale: three-level penthouses with roof terraces, 4-5 bedrooms.

about.caveat: "Sought after" is agent opinion, not market data. No price-per-type analysis was done.

types.layout: T ype 10 is the layout of all eight of the houses in Lambert Jones Mews. This is a terrace of two-storey mews houses with doors and garages onto a cobbled mews below Lauderdale Place. Lambert Jones Mews is genuinely a mews – while Brandon Mews is not – because it has a garage on the ground floor. An original mews house had the horses and carriage on the ground floor and the grooms lived above. The stabling was then converted into an integral garage in the modern mews house. So a proper mews house has a garage on the ground floor. As a matter of historical interest, ‘mews’ relates to birds not horses. Henry VIII kept falcons. When they were moulting or ‘mewing’ each year they were kept in ‘mews’ in the Strand. When he later moved his falcons out and his horses in, the ‘mews’ name stuck.
